name: tresk
author: rule-family designer (world: a string of 6-10 coloured beads; lineup answer)
description: BEAD-STRING RULE-FAMILY class in the LINEUP format (docs/RULE_FAMILIES.md revision 2, 2026-09-05; brainstorm in challenges/lab/NOTES_rules_beads.md; v1 kept as tresk.v1.json). CLUE = 2 or 3 example bead strings, one per line, letters from R/G/B, 6-10 beads each, all of different lengths; then a BLANK LINE; then FOUR candidate strings, one per line, all of the same length. ANSWER = the one candidate that obeys the hidden rule, written back verbatim (whitespace-insensitive, case-insensitive) or as its 1-based index 1-4. Exactly one candidate obeys the rule; the floor is therefore 25 %, and there is no 'freshness' clause of any kind (v1's unused-length rule is GONE - revision 2 sec.5). WHY THE LINEUP: in the first arena both Opus teams cracked v1 (97 % / 47 %) without ever naming a rule, by keeping every predicate of a ~300-strong pool that was true of all the examples and emitting a string that satisfied all of them at once - the true rule is in the pool, so the answer satisfies it by construction. A choice cannot be constructed: the player must say WHICH string is right, and the decoys are built so that every generic statistic points nowhere. UNIVERSE U (unchanged from v1): 8 templates, 38 concrete rules over f(w) = (#R, #G, #B, longest block, number of blocks, length, palindrome, #colours, all blocks the same size). (a) exactly n red/green/blue beads, n in 2..5; (b) the longest block of one colour is exactly n beads, n in 2..5; (c) exactly n blocks, n in 3..7; (d) the string is n beads long, n in 6..10; (e) it reads the same backwards; (f) only two colours are used; (g) all the blocks are the same size; (h) as many R as G / R as B / B as G; (i) all the X beads come before all the Y beads (both present), 6 ordered pairs. Only 23 of the 38 may be the HIDDEN rule (a random string of a random length satisfies it with probability <= 0.20); the other 15 - the loose counts 2 and 3, longest block 2 and 3, 5 and 6 blocks, and all five length rules - stay in U as COMPETITORS the examples must kill, which is what forces the examples to have different lengths. U is an ANTICHAIN (brute-forced over all 88209 strings of length 6-10), otherwise positive examples could never separate its rules. GENERATE draws the template uniformly, then a parameter, then one example per length from a set of distinct lengths, keeping the set only if exactly one rule of U survives and no proper subset of the examples already pins it (uniqueness + minimality, both 500/500). It then builds the LINEUP: it picks a length L, samples strings of that length that BREAK the rule, groups them by which excluded rules they happen to satisfy, and picks the true candidate from the rule's satisfiers so that it satisfies EXACTLY THE SAME excluded rules as its three decoys - so no trap, and no count of traps, separates them - and so that its rank in the OUTSIDE PREDICATE COUNT (how many of the 249 generic bead predicates that are consistent with every example it satisfies; that pool is the attacking player's, rebuilt bit-for-bit inside generate) is spread evenly over the four places. Measured: the true candidate is the top scorer on that count in 43 % of clues and 'pick the candidate that satisfies the most of my predicates' scores 39.0 % (revision 2 sec.2 asks for <= 60 %); its inverse scores 20.8 %; the medoid and the outlier by mutual Hamming distance score 25.2 % and 25.1 %. DELIBERATELY EXCLUDED RULES (never in U; the decoys' sponsors): 'no block is longer than the longest block in the clue' and 'at least n C beads (the clue's minimum)' - the loose cousins of templates b and a, consistent with 100 % of clues; 'exactly the same set of colours as the examples' 51 %; 'all three colours appear' 49 %; 'no two C beads ever touch' 24-27 %; 'more X beads than Y' 9-14 %; 'starts with / ends with the clue's colour' 19 % / 22 %; 'the two end beads are the same colour' 16 %; 'it alternates' 9 %. Mean 7.15 of them are consistent with the examples of any one clue and EVERY decoy fires at least one (500/500) - but because the true candidate fires exactly the same ones, a player who commits to any excluded rule is left picking at random: each of those rows scores exactly 25.0 %. The lesson of the class is unchanged - it only ever makes TIGHT statements (exactly n, the longest block IS 4, as many R as G, reads the same backwards) and never loose ones - but it is now worth 75 points instead of 84: knowing which rules are excluded no longer helps, only knowing which are USED does. WITNESSES over 500 fresh clues: pick candidate 1 25.8 %; a random candidate 25.0 %; the candidate satisfying the most example-consistent outside predicates 39.0 %; the fewest 20.8 %; the medoid 25.2 %; the outlier 25.1 %; each of the 19 excluded rules exactly 25.0 %; a player whose universe is U plus the excluded rules, committing to a random survivor, 34.8 %; a player who knows U minus its two rarest templates 80.7 %; the in-U intersection (a player who knows U) 100 %; the true rule 100 % (and 100 % answering by index). True-candidate position over 500 clues: 129 / 125 / 124 / 122. SOLVE re-derives the survivor exactly as the scorer does and returns the candidate that obeys it (there is nothing left to vary: the answer is a choice). SCORE is 805 chars (needs max_score_code_chars = 1024, the raise RULE_FAMILIES.md sec.4 allows for this paradigm): it splits the clue on the blank line, resolves an index or a verbatim candidate, rebuilds all 38 rules of U, filters them by the examples, insists on a single survivor and checks that the CHOSEN CANDIDATE obeys it - a string that is not in the lineup scores 0, which is what kills the construction attack. No hidden channel.
solve:
def solve(clue):
    B = clue.strip().split("\n\n")
    E = B[0].split("\n")
    K = B[1].split("\n")
    U =  [(0, i, n) for i in (0, 1, 2) for n in (2, 3, 4, 5)]
    U += [(0, 3, n) for n in (2, 3, 4, 5)]
    U += [(0, 4, n) for n in (3, 4, 5, 6, 7)]
    U += [(0, 5, n) for n in (6, 7, 8, 9, 10)]
    U += [(0, 6, 1), (0, 7, 2), (0, 8, 1), (1, 0, 1), (1, 0, 2), (1, 2, 1)]
    U += [(2, i, j) for i in (0, 1, 2) for j in (0, 1, 2) if i != j]

    def f(w):
        G = [len(list(g)) for _, g in itertools.groupby(w)]
        return [w.count(x) for x in "RGB"] + [max(G), len(G), len(w),
                w == w[::-1], len(set(w)), len(set(G)) == 1]

    def p(r, w):
        t, i, j = r
        g = f(w)
        if t < 1:
            return g[i] == j
        if t < 2:
            return g[i] == g[j]
        x = "RGB"[i]
        y = "RGB"[j]
        return x in w and y in w and w.rfind(x) < w.find(y)

    V = [r for r in U if all(p(r, e) for e in E)]
    for k in K:                    # exactly one candidate obeys the surviving rule
        if p(V[0], k):
            return k
    return K[0]
